analogy.p: Imagine two friends living at houses A and B who want a fence exactly halfway between them: every spot on the fence is the same distance from both houses, and the fence runs at right angles to the straight line joining them. That is the perpendicular bisector. A goat tied to a post by a rope can reach exactly the points inside a circle around the post, which is the locus of 'within a fixed distance of a point'. Both pictures show that a locus is just 'all the places that obey a rule'. The analogy breaks down because real friends measure fairness by the length of the road they walk, whereas a locus uses straight-line distance, and a rope can be blocked by a wall while the mathematical circle ignores obstacles.
analogy.t: The fair-fence and the goat on a rope

bullets: **Construct** means use compasses and a straight edge; the arcs must stay visible. A ruler and protractor will not earn the construction marks.
The three standard constructions are: **perpendicular bisector**, **angle bisector** and **perpendicular from/at a point**.
A **locus** (plural **loci**) is the set of all points that obey a given rule; you must be able to draw it and shade the **region** it describes.
Loci questions combine two or more rules, so you need to be fluent in the four basic loci (circle, track around a line, perpendicular bisector, angle bisector).
You must **know and use** that the shortest distance from a point to a line is the **perpendicular distance**.
Scale drawings and **bearings** link in: many loci questions give distances in metres or kilometres that must be converted using the scale.
Higher tier extension: finding the **circumcentre** and **incentre** of a triangle by constructing bisectors, and reasoning about whether a region exists at all.
core.p: Edexcel 1MA1 (Geometry and measures) expects you to **use the standard ruler and compass constructions**: the **perpendicular bisector of a line segment**, **constructing a perpendicular to a given line from a point or at a point**, and **bisecting a given angle**. You must then **use these constructions to build given figures and to solve loci problems**, and you must **know that the perpendicular distance from a point to a line is the shortest distance to the line**. Questions are worth about 2 to 4 marks, appear on Papers 1, 2 and 3 (they are often on the non-calculator paper because only a ruler and compasses are needed), and Higher papers like to hide the constructions inside a real-life context such as a garden, a radio mast or a treasure hunt.

bullets: Use a **sharp pencil**, a clear plastic ruler and compasses with a locked radius; do **not** use pen for construction lines.
**Never rub out construction arcs.** They are the evidence for the method marks (usually one M mark for the arcs, one A mark for the line).
Make arcs long enough that the two arcs clearly **cross**; tiny arcs make intersections hard to judge.
Use a **radius larger than half the length** of the line when bisecting it; otherwise the arcs will not meet.
Keep the **same compass setting** for both arcs in a pair (the two arcs from A and B; the two arcs from P and Q).
Extend the final line well beyond the arcs so the perpendicular or bisector is easy to see and check.
Label key points (A, B, P, Q, M) lightly, and write a cross or letter for the final answer if the question asks you to mark a position.
core.h: Equipment, accuracy and what examiners need to see
core.p: Constructions are marked on **method evidence**, not just the final line. The examiner is looking for the **construction arcs** that prove you used compasses, so they must never be rubbed out. A sharp pencil makes thin, accurate lines, and a pair of compasses that does not slip (tighten the screw!) keeps your radius constant. Mark schemes usually accept a small tolerance (typically about 2 mm on length and 2 degrees on angles), but arcs must be clearly drawn and intersect properly. If you draw the final line by eye through two wrong points, the accuracy mark is lost even if the line looks nearly right.

bullets: Step 1: open the compasses to more than half of AB (as a guide, about three-quarters of the length).
Step 2: with the point on **A**, draw an arc above AB and an arc below AB.
Step 3: **keep the radius the same**, put the point on **B**, and draw arcs above and below to cross the first pair at **P** and **Q**.
Step 4: join **P to Q** with a ruler; extend it past the arcs.
Result: PQ **bisects** AB (AM = MB) and is **perpendicular** to AB (angle AMP = 90 degrees).
If you need the midpoint of AB only, the point M where PQ crosses AB is the answer.
The construction also gives the **locus of points equidistant from A and B**.
core.h: Construction 1: the perpendicular bisector of a line segment
core.p: The **perpendicular bisector** of a line segment AB is the line that cuts AB into two equal halves **and** meets it at **90 degrees**. To construct it, set the compasses to a radius that is **more than half of AB**. With the point on A, draw an arc above and below the line. Without changing the radius, put the point on B and draw a second pair of arcs so that they **cross** the first pair above and below AB at P and Q. Finally use a ruler to join P and Q. The line PQ is the perpendicular bisector, and it crosses AB at the midpoint M.

bullets: Any point on the perpendicular bisector is **equidistant** from A and B (it is the locus of such points).
A point on the **A side** of the line is **closer to A**; a point on the B side is closer to B; this is how you decide which region to shade for 'nearer to A than B'.
The shape A-P-B-Q is a **rhombus**, and its diagonals are PQ and AB, which cross at 90 degrees.
The same idea shows that the perpendicular bisector of a **chord** of a circle passes through the **centre** of the circle.
Triangles APM and BPM are congruent (right angle, shared side PM, AP = BP), so AM = MB.
This is a fully reasoned fact you can quote in a proof: 'P is the same distance from A and B because the arcs have equal radius'.
core.p: The arcs from A and B have the same radius, so P is the **same distance from A as from B**, and so is Q. That makes AP = BP = AQ = BQ, so the four points A, P, B, Q form a **rhombus** (a shape with four equal sides). The diagonals of a rhombus **bisect each other at right angles**, which is why PQ is perpendicular to AB and passes through its midpoint. Another way to see it is that triangles APQ and BPQ are **congruent (SSS)**, which gives equal angles at P and means every point on PQ is equidistant from A and B. Knowing the reason matters because it tells you what the line **means** in a loci question: the points exactly as far from A as from B.

bullets: Step 1: point on the **vertex O**, draw an arc cutting **both arms** (call the cut points P and Q).
Step 2: with the point on **P**, draw an arc inside the angle.
Step 3: with the point on **Q** and **the same radius**, draw an arc crossing the first at **R**.
Step 4: draw a straight line from **O through R**; extend it.
Check: the two new angles should each be half the original; you can measure with a protractor as a check but **do not** use the protractor to draw it.
The construction works for **any** angle, including reflex or obtuse angles (as long as the arcs cross).
If you are asked to bisect the angle of a triangle, use the vertex as O and the two sides as the arms.
core.p: To **bisect an angle** means to split it into two **equal angles**. Take angle POQ with vertex O. Place the compass point on **O** and draw an arc that crosses **both arms**, at P and Q. Keep the same radius or choose a new one (it just needs to be big enough), and from P and then from Q draw two arcs that **cross each other** at R inside the angle; the radius for these two arcs must be the **same**. Finally join **O to R** and extend it. The line OR is the **angle bisector**, making two angles that are each half of the original.

bullets: The reason is **congruent triangles (SSS)**: OP = OQ, PR = QR, OR common.
Every point on the bisector is **equidistant from the two arms** (perpendicular distances are equal).
A point on the side of the bisector nearer to one arm is **closer to that arm**; this decides which side to shade.
The bisector of angle A in a rectangle corner meets the sides at **45 degrees**, which gives the diagonal line used in garden-style questions.
Bisecting a 60 degree angle gives **30 degrees**, and bisecting 90 degrees gives **45 degrees**.
In a triangle, the three angle bisectors meet at the **incentre**, the centre of the inscribed circle (Higher extension).
core.p: The first arc has radius OP = OQ because it was drawn from O. The arcs from P and Q have equal radii, so PR = QR. Then triangles OPR and OQR have **three equal sides** (OP = OQ, PR = QR, and OR shared), so they are **congruent (SSS)**. Congruent triangles have equal corresponding angles, so angle POR = angle QOR, and OR splits the angle exactly in half. The consequence for loci is that every point on the bisector is the **same perpendicular distance from both arms**, which is why the angle bisector is the locus of points **equidistant from two lines**.

bullets: Step 1: point on **P**, draw an arc crossing the line at **X** and **Y**.
Step 2: from **X** and **Y** with equal radii, draw arcs that cross on the other side of the line (below it if P is above).
Step 3: join **P** to the crossing point; the line meets the original line at 90 degrees.
The distance **PF** is the **shortest distance** from P to the line.
The method is really the perpendicular bisector of the chord XY, because P is equidistant from X and Y.
The construction is used to find the **nearest point on a road, river or wall** to a given point, and to draw heights of triangles.
Draw the line long enough so the right angle at F can be seen and checked.
core.h: Construction 3: the perpendicular from a point to a line
core.p: Sometimes you are given a line and a point **P not on the line** and must draw the line through P at **90 degrees** to it. Put the compass point on **P** and draw an arc that cuts the given line at **two points X and Y**; the radius must be big enough to reach the line twice. Then, from X and then from Y, using the **same radius** (large enough that the arcs cross), draw arcs on the opposite side of the line from P so they meet. Join P to the meeting point with a ruler. This line is perpendicular to the given line, and the point F where it meets the line is the **foot of the perpendicular**.

bullets: Step 1: point on **P**, mark **X and Y** either side of P on the line (equal distances from P).
Step 2: **increase the radius** a little, and from X and Y draw arcs that cross above (or below) the line.
Step 3: join the crossing point to **P**; this line is at **90 degrees** to the original line at P.
This is the same construction as the perpendicular bisector, applied to the segment XY with midpoint P.
You can use it to build a **right angle** at the end of a line (extend the line first so you have room on both sides).
Squares, rectangles and right-angled triangles in construction questions are built from this step.
If the line is too short to put X and Y on both sides, extend it with a ruler first.
core.h: Construction 4: the perpendicular at a point on a line
core.p: If the point P **lies on the line**, you cannot draw an arc that cuts the line twice from P itself, so you create the two points yourself. Put the compass point on **P** and draw a small arc cutting the line on **both sides** at X and Y; these are the same distance from P. Then bisect XY by drawing equal arcs from X and from Y (with a larger radius) so that they cross above the line. Join P to that crossing point. Because P is the midpoint of XY, the line you drew is the **perpendicular bisector of XY** and therefore meets the line at P at **90 degrees**. This is also the standard way to construct a right angle.

bullets: Shortest distance = **perpendicular distance** from the point to the line.
Reason: any slanted path is the **hypotenuse** of a right-angled triangle, so it is longer than the perpendicular side (Pythagoras).
To find it by construction: draw the perpendicular from the point, then **measure** it and convert using the scale.
The perpendicular meets the line at the **foot** F, the nearest point on the line.
The same idea gives: a **tangent** to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
In a loci question 'within 5 m of the path', the track is drawn by measuring perpendicular distances from the path.
For a point to be 'within d of a line', its perpendicular distance must be at most d.
core.h: Shortest distance from a point to a line
core.p: The **shortest distance** from a point to a line is the **perpendicular distance**, measured along the line that meets the given line at 90 degrees. Any other route from the point to the line is longer because it forms the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle whose other side is the perpendicular; by Pythagoras the hypotenuse is always the longest side. In practice, you construct the perpendicular from the point (Construction 3) and then measure its length with a ruler. This idea underlies questions such as 'find the nearest point on the road to the house' or 'how close does the ship come to the lighthouse'.

bullets: **60 degrees**: equilateral triangle, three arcs of equal radius, all sides equal.
**30 degrees**: bisect 60 degrees. **45 degrees**: bisect 90 degrees. **120 degrees**: two adjacent 60 degree angles.
**SSS triangle**: draw the longest side as a base, then from each end draw an arc with the other side lengths; the arcs cross at the third vertex.
**SAS triangle**: draw one side, measure the angle with a protractor at one end, mark the second side length along that direction, then join.
**ASA triangle**: draw the given side, measure the two angles at its ends and extend the lines until they meet.
Keep construction arcs when the question says 'using ruler and compasses'; use a protractor only when angles are given as measurements.
Always check your finished shape by measuring it against the given lengths.
core.h: Building other angles and shapes from constructions
core.p: Once you can bisect and draw perpendiculars you can build many angles using compasses only. A **60 degree angle** is made by drawing an **equilateral triangle**: draw a line AB, then from A and from B draw arcs with radius AB that cross at C, so triangle ABC has three equal sides and every angle is 60 degrees. Bisect it for **30 degrees**, construct a perpendicular for **90 degrees**, bisect that for **45 degrees**, and add 60 and 30 to make **90** or add 60 and 60 for **120 degrees**. You may also be asked to construct **triangles** from given side lengths, using ruler and compasses (SSS) or from two sides and an included angle (SAS) or two angles and a side (ASA) using a ruler and protractor.

bullets: **Fixed distance from a point C:** a **circle** of that radius centred on C.
**Fixed distance from a line segment:** a **rounded rectangle** (parallel lines at that distance plus semicircular ends).
**Equidistant from two points A and B:** the **perpendicular bisector** of AB.
**Equidistant from two lines:** the **angle bisector** of the angle between them.
**Fixed distance from an infinite line:** two parallel lines either side at that distance.
**Loci** is the plural of locus; examiners write 'draw the locus of...'.
A locus can be a **line** (equidistant) or a **region** (nearer to / within / at least).
core.p: A **locus** is the set of **all points** that obey a given rule, usually drawn as a line, curve or region. You should know four basic loci. The locus of points at a **fixed distance from a point** is a **circle**. The locus of points at a **fixed distance from a straight line segment** is a **track**: two parallel lines with semicircular ends. The locus of points **equidistant from two points** is the **perpendicular bisector** of the line joining them. The locus of points **equidistant from two intersecting lines** is the **angle bisector** of the angle between them. Every loci problem is made from these building blocks.

bullets: Draw each locus as a **boundary** first; keep the arcs and construction lines.
'**Within** d' / 'no more than d' means **inside** the circle or track; 'at least d' / 'further than d' means **outside**.
'**Nearer to A than B**' = the side of the perpendicular bisector containing A.
'**Closer to line 1 than line 2**' = the side of the angle bisector next to line 1.
Shade the **intersection** (the region meeting all conditions); some questions ask for 'the region R' labelled.
Check with a **test point**: choose a point in the shaded area and confirm every condition holds.
Stay inside any shape boundary given (a garden, field or rectangle); a region cannot extend outside it.
If the conditions cannot all be met, the region is empty: say so and explain using distances.
core.p: Most exam questions ask for a **region** that satisfies two or more conditions. Draw each boundary locus accurately, then decide which side of each boundary satisfies the condition, and **shade only the overlap**. Words matter: **'within 3 m of A'** means inside or on the circle of radius 3 m; **'at least 3 m from A'** means outside or on it; **'nearer to A than to B'** means the A side of the perpendicular bisector; **'closer to AB than AD'** means the side of the angle bisector nearer to AB. Test a point in the region you shade: pick a point, measure its distances, and check it truly satisfies every condition.

bullets: **Convert real distances to drawing lengths** using the scale before you draw a circle or measure.
Bearings are measured **clockwise from north**, with **three figures**; use a protractor at the point with a north line.
State measured results in **real units** (metres, km), with the scale used.
If a scale is given as a ratio 1 : 50 000, then 1 cm represents 50 000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km.
Typical contexts: radio mast reach, sprinkler region, guard dog on a rope, ship distance from a lighthouse.
When something is 'tied to a post' or on a 'rope', the locus is a **circle** (or part of one if blocked by a wall).
Label the point you are asked for with a **cross** and give its position if asked.
core.h: Loci in context: scale drawings, maps and bearings
core.p: Real-life loci questions give a **scale** (for example 1 cm represents 2 km) and distances in real units, so you must **convert lengths** before measuring or drawing. If the radius of a circle is 6 km and the scale is 1 cm : 2 km, then you draw a circle of **6 divided by 2 = 3 cm** radius. Some questions give **bearings** (angles measured clockwise from north, written with three figures such as 065 degrees) to place a point; use a protractor from the north line. Always state the final answer in the **real units** of the question, and show the conversion in your working when marks are allocated for method.

bullets: **Circumcentre:** meeting point of the three **perpendicular bisectors**; equidistant from the **vertices**.
**Incentre:** meeting point of the three **angle bisectors**; equidistant from the **sides**.
To find the **centre of a circle** from the circle alone: draw two chords and construct their perpendicular bisectors; they meet at the centre.
The **radius to a tangent is perpendicular** to the tangent, and the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
Only two perpendicular bisectors are needed to find the circumcentre; the third is a check.
If asked to 'find the point equidistant from three towns', construct perpendicular bisectors of two sides of the triangle they form.
core.h: Constructions in circles and triangles (Higher links)
core.p: Constructions connect to circle geometry and triangle centres. The **perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre of the circle**, so two chords' perpendicular bisectors meet at the centre. For a triangle, the three **perpendicular bisectors of the sides** meet at the **circumcentre**, which is the same distance from all three vertices, so a circle centred there passes through them all (the **circumcircle**). The three **angle bisectors** meet at the **incentre**, equidistant from the three sides, so a circle centred there touches all three sides (the **incircle**). Being able to explain the meaning of each bisector as a locus is a typical Higher reasoning skill.

bullets: Draw **construction arcs boldly enough to be seen** but thin enough to be accurate.
Mark the **final answer** (line, region or position) clearly: shade it, label it, or mark with a cross.
Show **conversion of the scale** in a line of working; this often carries a method mark.
Use **measurements** with units; a correct measured distance within tolerance earns the accuracy mark.
If the diagram is already drawn for you, **do the construction on it**; do not redraw it.
Check at the end: does every condition in the question appear in your drawing?
core.h: Presenting your answer and mark scheme technique
core.p: Examiners award marks for the **method** (the construction arcs) and for **accuracy** (the final line or region). Typical allocations are 2 marks for a single construction (M1 arcs, A1 line) and 3 to 4 marks for a loci problem (for example 1 mark for each correct locus and 1 for the correct region). Because the arcs are the proof, **leave all construction lines in place**. Make sure the final region is **clearly shaded or labelled R** and that nothing extra is shaded. If asked to **explain or show** something (for example that a point is impossible) use distances in words or numbers, not just a drawing.

exam: **Construct** means compasses and a ruler: keep all arcs. A construction is usually **2 marks**: M1 for correct arcs, A1 for the correct line.
For a **4-mark loci** question expect about 1 mark per correct locus (circle, bisector, etc.) and 1 mark for the correctly shaded region.
**Shade** only the region that meets **all** conditions; label it **R** if asked.
Quote the **meaning** if asked to explain: 'every point on this line is the same distance from A and B'.
For scale questions, show the conversion: **real distance divided by scale** gives the drawing length.
For 'within' use **inside the circle**; for 'at least' use **outside**; check with a test point.
If the problem asks 'is it possible?', compare distances: the **perpendicular distance** from the point to the line against the radius.
If the shape is drawn for you, do the construction **on that shape**; examiners compare with a template.
**Tolerance** is typically about 2 mm and 2 degrees, so draw carefully with a sharp pencil.
Check the final answer includes **units** when a measurement is asked for (for example metres).

mistakes.r: The arcs are the evidence of the method; leaving them in is required to earn the method mark.
mistakes.w: Rubbing out the construction arcs to make the diagram look neat.

mistakes.r: Both arcs from A and B (and from P and Q) must use the same radius or the line will not be the true bisector.
mistakes.w: Changing the compass radius between the two arcs of a pair.

mistakes.r: The radius must be greater than half of AB so the arcs cross.
mistakes.w: Using a radius less than half of AB.

mistakes.r: A construction uses compasses and a straight edge; a protractor-drawn line will not score the construction marks.
mistakes.w: Measuring and drawing with a protractor when asked to construct.

mistakes.r: Equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector (a straight line), not a circle.
mistakes.w: Drawing a circle for 'equidistant from A and B'.

mistakes.r: Test a point: 'within' is inside the circle; 'nearer to A' is the A side of the perpendicular bisector.
mistakes.w: Shading the wrong side for 'nearer to A than B' or 'within 3 m'.

mistakes.r: Convert real distance to drawing length using the scale first (6 km at 1 cm : 2 km is 3 cm).
mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert the scale (drawing a 6 cm radius for 6 km).

mistakes.r: The shortest distance is the perpendicular distance, so construct the perpendicular and measure that.
mistakes.w: Measuring the shortest distance along a slanted line.

summary: The specification asks you to construct a perpendicular bisector, an angle bisector and a perpendicular to a line using compasses, to use these to draw loci, and to know that the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance. It matters because loci and construction questions are worth several marks on every paper and reward careful method.

terms.d: The set of all points that satisfy a given rule or condition (plural: loci).
Draw accurately using a straight edge and compasses (and a protractor only when angles are given), keeping the construction arcs visible.
At right angles (90 degrees) to a line.
A line that cuts a line segment into two equal parts at 90 degrees.
A line from the vertex that divides an angle into two equal angles.
The same distance from two or more points or lines.
Part of the circumference of a circle.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its circumference; the compass setting.
The part of a line between two end points.
The point where two lines or edges meet to form an angle.
An area of the diagram containing all the points that satisfy the conditions.
A straight line joining two points on a circle.
The point where the three perpendicular bisectors of a triangle meet; equidistant from the three vertices.
The point where the three angle bisectors of a triangle meet; equidistant from the three sides.
The ratio of a length on a drawing to the real length, for example 1 cm : 2 km.
An angle measured clockwise from north, written with three figures.

worked.ans: The line PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB: M1 for correct arcs from both ends with equal radius, A1 for the line through the intersections; it meets AB at its midpoint at 90 degrees.
worked.q: (2 marks) Line AB has length 7 cm. Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB.
steps: Open the compasses to a radius greater than 3.5 cm (half of 7 cm), for example 5 cm.
Put the point on A and draw an arc above and below AB.
Keep the radius the same, put the point on B, and draw arcs above and below that cross the first two arcs at P and Q.
Use a ruler to join P and Q and extend the line past the arcs.
Leave all arcs in place; the line crosses AB at its midpoint, 3.5 cm from A, at 90 degrees.

worked.ans: The shaded region is the 45 degree sector with centre A, radius 3 cm, lying between AB and the angle bisector: 1 mark circle, 1 mark bisector construction, 1 mark correct side, 1 mark correct region.
worked.q: (4 marks) ABCD is a rectangle 6 m by 4 m, drawn with scale 1 cm : 1 m (AB = 6 cm, AD = 4 cm). Shade the region of points that are within 3 m of A and closer to AB than to AD.
steps: Convert: 3 m at 1 cm : 1 m is a radius of 3 cm.
Draw an arc of radius 3 cm centred on A (inside the rectangle) to show the locus 'within 3 m of A'.
Bisect angle DAB (90 degrees) with compasses to draw the 45 degree line from A; points on it are equidistant from AB and AD.
Decide the side: closer to AB is the side nearer to AB, below the bisector (towards AB).
Shade the region inside the arc and below the bisector, a sector of angle 45 degrees and radius 3 cm.

worked.ans: No, it is not possible: the nearest point equidistant from A and B is 8 km from A, which is more than 6 km.
worked.q: (3 marks) Towns A and B are 8 cm apart on a map with scale 1 cm : 2 km. A phone mast must be the same distance from A and B and within 6 km of A. Is this possible?
steps: Equidistant from A and B means on the perpendicular bisector of AB, which crosses AB at its midpoint M.
AM = 8 cm divided by 2 = 4 cm, and the bisector is perpendicular to AB, so M is the nearest point of the bisector to A.
So the shortest distance from A to the bisector is 4 cm, which is 4 x 2 = 8 km.
Within 6 km of A is a circle of radius 6 divided by 2 = 3 cm; the circle only reaches 3 cm from A.
Since 8 km is greater than 6 km (4 cm is greater than 3 cm), the circle never touches the bisector.
